purpose: Authored deterministic multiple-choice assessments for Weeks 16-20 of the Learn → Apply → Check → Evidence pathway.
grading: Each question uses one module-authored correctIndex. Choice scoring is deterministic; all questions in the set must be correct to pass.

questions.prompt: An MCC physically fits, but cable termination access is poor. What is the strongest senior response?
options: Accept it because the equipment fits.
Treat access and maintainability as design constraints and revise the arrangement before issue.
Move the issue to the construction team without documenting it.

questions.prompt: A new MCC feeder is added. Which set of records should be coordinated?
options: Only the MCC GA.
The GA, SLD, cable schedule, protection information, interfaces and revision/change records.
Only the equipment tag.

questions.prompt: When should a switchboard layout assumption be escalated?
options: Only when the drawing no longer looks balanced.
When it affects safety, equipment interface, maintainability, compliance or a vendor/engineer approval boundary.
Never; layout assumptions are always drafting-only matters.

questions.prompt: A board extension changes available cable termination space. What should be checked before issue?
options: Only the overall board width.
Termination access, cable entry, bend space, equipment interfaces and affected documentation.
Only the title block revision.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence of a coordinated switchboard layout?
options: A visually tidy GA only.
A checked layout showing interfaces, access constraints, coordinated tags and traceable dispositions for outstanding issues.
A screenshot of the 3D model with no revision context.

questions.prompt: A field instrument exists on the P&ID but not in the electrical I/O list. What is the strongest response?
options: Add a guessed I/O point and continue.
Record the interface discrepancy, trace the controlled source and coordinate the intended signal before finalizing documentation.
Ignore it because the P&ID is not an electrical drawing.

questions.prompt: Why should power and signal interfaces remain clearly separated?
options: They have different design, segregation, termination and verification considerations.
It makes drawings use more symbols.
They can never share a panel.

questions.prompt: What should be confirmed before assigning a PLC termination?
options: Only the device colour.
Signal type, source, destination, I/O ownership, termination arrangement and approved control philosophy.
Only the nearest terminal number.

questions.prompt: A control signal appears on two different I/O lists with conflicting destinations. What should happen?
options: Pick the destination that is easiest to draw.
Reconcile the authoritative control philosophy and interface ownership before finalizing the termination documentation.
Duplicate the signal on both lists without clarification.

questions.prompt: What makes an I/O documentation change issue-ready?
options: Only assigning a terminal number.
Traceable source/destination, signal definition, ownership, termination and confirmation against the approved control basis.
A completed title block regardless of content.

questions.prompt: A cable length is uncertain and voltage drop is close to the project limit. What is the strongest response?
options: Use the shortest likely length and finalize the cable.
Confirm the route/length, document the assumption and reassess before final selection.
Ignore the uncertainty because the result is only slightly over the limit.

questions.prompt: Which inputs should be traceable in a cable-sizing calculation?
options: Load/current, length, installation method, correction factors/conditions, allowable voltage drop and design assumptions.
Cable colour and drawing scale only.
Only the preferred manufacturer.

questions.prompt: When should a calculation result be escalated?
options: Never if the spreadsheet produces a number.
When inputs are incomplete, the result is marginal, or engineering judgement/approval is required.
Only after the drawing is issued.

questions.prompt: A cable installation method changes after the original sizing check. What is the correct response?
options: Keep the original result because the cable size is already selected.
Reassess the calculation using the revised installation conditions and update affected documentation.
Change only the cable note without recalculating.

questions.prompt: What makes a cable-sizing result suitable for senior review?
options: A final cable size with no assumptions.
Traceable inputs, method, governing criteria, assumptions, result and clear indication of any approval or verification boundary.
Only a screenshot of a spreadsheet cell.

questions.prompt: A drawing looks correct but its cable schedule contradicts it. How should the checker respond?
options: Accept the drawing because it looks correct.
Raise the traceability issue, identify affected documents and require resolution before issue.
Correct the schedule silently without recording the change.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an effective checking comment?
options: It is as short as possible, even if unclear.
It identifies the issue, consequence or required clarification clearly enough for the designer to act.
It only states that something is wrong.

questions.prompt: When is a package not ready for closure?
options: When significant technical, safety, compliance, interface or traceability issues remain unresolved.
Whenever a checker has any comment, regardless of severity.
Only when the title block is incomplete.

questions.prompt: A checker finds several comments caused by one missing design input. What is the strongest response?
options: Close each comment independently without addressing the cause.
Identify the common missing input, resolve or escalate it, then reassess the affected comments and documents.
Remove the comments to keep the review concise.

questions.prompt: What should a senior checker preserve when accepting a correction?
options: Only the corrected drawing.
The issue disposition and enough traceability to show what changed, why it was accepted and what was rechecked.
Nothing once the PDF is exported.

questions.prompt: A redline is unclear but could affect cable routing. What is the strongest response?
options: Interpret it using the most convenient routing.
Raise a clarification before incorporation and record the potential downstream impact.
Delete the markup and continue.

questions.prompt: Why assess change impact before editing a redline?
options: Because one change can affect multiple drawings, schedules, references and design assumptions.
Because revisions are only administrative.
Because every drawing must be completely redrawn.

questions.prompt: What closes a revision properly?
options: Only changing the revision letter.
Incorporating the change, checking affected documents, updating revision information and recording unresolved items.
Printing the marked-up drawing.

questions.prompt: A redline changes an equipment tag used across several documents. What should happen?
options: Update only the marked-up drawing.
Trace the tag across affected documents and update them consistently through the controlled revision workflow.
Leave the other documents unchanged until construction.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence that a redline change was fully incorporated?
options: The redline is no longer visible.
The change is incorporated, affected references/schedules are reconciled, revision records are updated and the resulting package has been checked.
The file has a new filename.
